To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the very neutron-rich nucleus C 20 has been studied by inelastic scattering of 12 C on 208 Pb, liquid hydrogen and 12 C targets.
The neutron transition probability M2n of the 20 C nucleus has been determined for the first time.
the valence neutrones of the carbon isotopes heavier that 14 C are decoupled from the nuclear core and that this decoupling is persistent up to the dripline.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the evolution of the structure of the carbon isotopes towards the neutron drip line.
the study of the evolution of the nuclear structure from the proton dripline to the neutron dripline.
the study of the evolution of the nuclear structure of carbon isotopes in the vicinity of the neutron dripline, and the development of the shell structure of the neutron-rich carbon isotopes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the valence neutrones in 20 C are not fully coupled to the core and this decoupling increases with neutron excess.
the 0 + g. s. → 2 + level is populated by the transfer of two valence neutrons, which are not strongly coupled to the core.
the valence neutrones in C20 are not coupled to the core, but rather are in a state that is decoupled from the core, which is the same as the case of the valence protons in 14 C.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the valence neutrones are decoupled from the core in the very neutron rich carbon isotopes.
the neutron-rich isotopes of carbon are the best candidates for studying the onset of the neutron dripline.
the neutron transition probabilities M 2 n of the ground-state band in the very neutron-rich carbon isotopes are systematically lower than those of the stable isotopes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the B(E2;0 + → 2 + ) of 20 C is much smaller than the systematics of the B(E2) values in carbon isotopes.
